title: Latency-tiered toolflow and payload contract PRD sketch
content:
Quick summary:
This PRD sketch proposes a latency-tiered model for the Hosted API SDK and stream protocol that exposes predictable latencies to clients while enabling structured tool calls and compact payload contracts. The goal is to make it straightforward for application teams to select an operating point (low-latency, mid-tier interactive, or high-throughput) and get consistent semantics for partial results, tool call handshakes, and typed outputs.

Problem we see in the wild:
- Apps try to balance interactive responsiveness vs completeness: mobile chat needs first-word latency < 120ms for snappy UX, while batch document synthesis tolerates seconds per token.
- Tool integrations (search, DB, calculators) are brittle: ad-hoc JSON blobs, no small stable schema for early results, and unclear retry semantics across intermittent networks.
- SDK ergonomics are inconsistent: some teams handle streaming frames manually, others re-request whole responses on failure.

Success metrics (measurable):
- 95th percentile first-byte latency under chosen tier for client requests (tier A: < 150ms, tier B: < 400ms, tier C: < 1s).
- Decrease in customer error/retry code paths for tool calls by 40% (tracked via SDK telemetry tag).
- Adoption: 25% of newly created Hosted API integrations using the new payload contract within 6 months.

Design overview (high level):
1) Latency tiers: API/SDK surface exposes a "latency_tier" param with values: fast, balanced, batch. Each tier implies server-side scheduling (priority queues, max batching window), streaming behaviour (frame flush frequency), and optional prefetch heuristics.
2) Compact payload contract: layered frame types with a small required core and extensible typed attachments. Core frames: BEGIN, DELTA, TOOL_CALL, TOOL_RESULT, END, ERROR. Each frame includes a small header: {request_id, seq, latency_tier, schema_version}. The payload body is either untyped text or a structured JSON blob when schema declared.
3) Tool-call lifecycle: explicit 3-way handshake for tool calls in streams: TOOL_CALL(frame) -> TOOL_ACK(frame) -> TOOL_RESULT(frame). TOOL_ACK must include an estimated resolution ETA and a tool-token to be used for retries; TOOL_RESULT contains typed result and a bitmask of optional fields present.
4) Partial structured output: SDK will provide helpers to progressively merge structured fragments into a final typed object (no partial JSON re-parsing by user). We define a minimal type system (strings, numbers, arrays, records) and patch operations (append, set, splice) encoded in DELTA frames so clients can apply deterministically.

SDK ergonomics (developer-facing):
- One-line integration: client.request({model, prompt, latency_tier: 'fast', onFrame}) returns an ergonomic handle. onFrame receives typed events mapped to high-level callbacks: onText, onToolCall, onToolProgress, onStructuredPatch, onComplete, onError.
- Backpressure and cancellation: SDK exposes cancel() and provide an expected latency SLO; server may respond with THROTTLE frames indicating temporary backoff with recommended retry-after.
- Local prefetch suggestions: server can send PREFETCH_HINT frames for likely next tokens or tool calls (used by client to warm caches). Hints are advisory and limited in size.

Failure modes and graceful degradation:
- Tool unavailability: TOOL_ACK with status=queued + ETA; if unfulfilled before timeout, server emits TOOL_RESULT with status=failed and fallback_text (if configured) or an automatic fallback model-generated answer.
- Partial-frame loss: seq numbers in headers allow SDK to detect gaps. For fast tier, SDK should surface a degraded chunk and optionally attempt low-cost rehydration; for balanced/batch tiers, SDK will attempt server-side resends.

Observability/telemetry:
- Telemetry keys to include in frames: request_id, latency_tier, model_family, token_count, tool_ids_used, frame_counts. SDKs will emit structured metrics to console (and propagate tokens to backend) to compute first-byte latency, tool call success rates, and patch-apply errors.

Experimentation plan:
- Phase 1 (4w): Implement server-side latency_tier scheduling with no SDK changes (legacy stream format). Run internal canaries for high-volume customers.
- Phase 2 (6w): Add frame headers and TOOL_CALL handshake in an opt-in preview SDK. Collect telemetry and iterate contract fields.
- Phase 3 (8w): Default SDK behavior, deprecate legacy untyped tool frames, provide migration tooling (cli to validate seqs and patch applications).

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- How big should headers be vs bandwidth sensitivity on mobile? Suggest base64-compact headers but allow optional verbose headers for debugging.
- Should PREFETCH_HINTs be allowed in fast tier (risk: network overhead) or restricted to balanced? Propose opt-in per client.
- Versioning: how to evolve typed attachments safely. Proposal: include schema_version in header and fallback to untyped text when schema unknown.

Migration notes for customers:
- Provide a converter: old stream events -> new framed events (server-side translation layer) for 3 months.
- SDK lint tool: static check for applying patches idempotently; sample code for JS/Go/Python.

Next steps (immediate owners):
- Product: finalize tier numeric SLOs and list of default models per tier (owner: Asha).
- Eng runtime: prototype compact header + seq resends (owner: Marco).
- SDK: implement frame parser and high-level callbacks in JS (owner: Lina).
- Solutions: draft migration playbook and sample app (owner: Devon).

Notes to self / rough thoughts:
- Keep tool handshake minimal to avoid latency tax on fast tier.
- Consider a separate small control channel (out-of-band) for tool ACKs to avoid stalling token stream when tools are slow.
- Link to earlier experiments: RED-2142 has prototype bench results for tier scheduling; see linked PR.

Unresolved TODOs:
- Decide default persistence semantics for TOOL_RESULT (should server store final tool outputs for replays?).
- Rate limit semantics per-account when using fast tier (prevent noisy neighbors).

Rough timeline: 4 months from approval to GA for core frame contract and SDK bits.

Document history: initial sketch 2024-10-03 by Asha Patel, first review 2024-10-15, engineering notes added 2024-11-05.
